project.name: PathCraft
project.tagline: Self-hosted multimodal routing engine (OSM + GTFS) with a plugin architecture and an embedded web directions app
project.status: working prototype / pre-release, single developer + AI-assisted

what_it_does: Parses OpenStreetMap extracts into a mode-aware street graph (walk/car/bike, oneway and access restrictions honored)
Parses full GTFS transit feeds and answers multimodal door-to-door journeys (walk + bus with transfers) via a RAPTOR-style algorithm
Serves a JSON/GeoJSON HTTP API: /route, /journey, /nearest (snap to road), /nodes (viewport intersections), /graph, /transit/*, /modes, /config
Ships a single Go binary with an embedded React SPA: Google-Maps-style directions UI (A/B picking, per-mode ETAs solved in parallel, transit itineraries, debug overlays)
Caches parsed OSM graphs to binary cache files for fast restarts

tech_stack.backend: Go 1.25.12, stdlib HTTP, zap logging, compile-time plugin registry (algorithms, graph loaders, exporters, cost models, loggers)
tech_stack.algorithms: A* for street routing, RAPTOR for transit timetables
tech_stack.frontend: React 19, Vite 8, UnoCSS, Leaflet/react-leaflet, TypeScript; embedded via go:embed
tech_stack.data_formats: OSM XML (Overpass extracts), GTFS static (stop_times, trips, stops, routes, shapes, transfers)
tech_stack.deployment_model: single self-contained binary + map tiles from any tile server (OSM default); no external routing APIs, no cloud dependencies

scale_proven.osm_graph: city-scale extract, binary cache ~9.4 MB, loads in seconds
scale_proven.gtfs_feed: official Grande Recife feed: 3,150,132 stop_times rows (180 MB), 87,579 trips, 7,143 stops, 30 MB shapes
scale_proven.gtfs_loading: chunked streaming parser with string interning; ~35 MB zip fetched via make fetch-gtfs
scale_proven.query_latency_observed: street route solve ~20 ms; multimodal journey with real feed returns sub-second; all four modes solved in parallel per request pair
scale_proven.example_real_result: 08:00 departure across Recife -> arrival 08:38, walk 358 m + bus with transfer, real trip IDs

quality_signals.tests: 93 Go tests across 28 packages + 19 frontend vitest tests; ESLint and tsc clean; fixtures in tracked testdata/ so suite passes from fresh clone
quality_signals.ci: GitHub Actions Go test workflow (frontend not yet in CI)
quality_signals.docs: architecture docs, plugin-system docs, roadmap, demo tutorial in docs/

differentiators: Single-binary, fully self-hosted alternative to Google Directions / Mapbox for orgs that cannot ship rider data to third parties
Plugin registry design: swap routing algorithms, cost models, exporters without forking the core
Handles real Brazilian transit feeds out of the box (proven on Grande Recife), a market underserved by polished routing tooling
Whole stack is inspectable: graph debug overlays (street classes, intersections, stops) built into the shipped UI
current_gaps_be_honest: No geocoding/search-by-name (coordinates and map clicks only)
GTFS calendar/service-day filtering not applied (all trips treated as running); no GTFS-realtime
No turn-by-turn instructions, no traffic, bike/car use heuristic speeds
Single-city testing; no horizontal scaling story, auth, rate limiting, or multi-tenant features
Router marked by author as debug/demo grade rather than production
No packaged releases, Docker image, or hosted demo yet
near_term_roadmap_hints: Frontend CI job, Docker packaging, hosted demo
Geocoder integration (e.g., Nominatim/Photon) for address search
More city feeds to prove generality (catalog of Brazilian capitals)
possible_business_surfaces_raw_facts_for: Transit agencies / city governments in Brazil publish GTFS but lack rider-facing journey planners they control
Logistics and delivery companies need self-hosted routing where per-request API pricing (Google: ~USD 5-10 per 1000 directions calls) dominates costs
Urban-planning consultancies need multimodal accessibility analysis on open data
White-label embedded directions widget for real-estate/tourism portals
The plugin architecture allows selling proprietary cost models (safety, accessibility, low-emission routing) on an open core
